summary: This RFC covers the implementation of domain name servers and resolvers, specifies the format of their messages, and discusses how domain names fit existing mail systems and network software. It is an early version of the DNS specification, replaced by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the instruction manual for building the phone book that turns names into numbers, including how the questions and answers are written down.

questions: how do dns servers and resolvers talk
how did the original dns work
what is an inverse query in dns
subtitle: The 1983 draft design for DNS name servers, resolvers, message formats and zone maintenance, later replaced by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

tldr.problem: Hosts on different networks needed one scheme for naming resources, and a way to look names up in a database spread over many servers.
tldr.mechanism: Resolvers ask name servers questions in a single message format of five sections. Name servers hold zones of authoritative data, cache the rest, and refresh copied zones from master servers.
tldr.outcome: The RFC itself warns that its formats are preliminary and not for real implementations. It was replaced by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 and updated by RFC 973.

today: RFC 883 is an early version of the DNS specification. It was obsoleted by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 and updated by RFC 973, so it should be read only as history.

sections.title: Resolvers, Name Servers and Zones
sections.content:
This memo, from November 1983, covers how to build name servers and resolvers, the format of their messages, and how domain names fit mail systems. It assumes the reader knows RFC 882. Its algorithms and data structures are suggestions; implementers may use their own as long as the external behavior is the same.

The RFC carries a warning: its format specifications are preliminary and included for purposes of explanation only, and nobody should use them for actual implementations.

To the user, the domain tree is a single information space. A resolver, the local agent a user program talks to, knows at least one name server. It either gets the answer or a referral to another server, and uses referrals to learn about more servers. Name servers hold zones, each the complete database for a subtree, called authoritative data, plus cached data that expires on a timeout.

The memo also states conventions: bytes are transmitted most significant first, and all comparisons of labels and names are case-insensitive, though the original case should be kept where possible. The CLASS field tags data so that programs can identify the format and guide queries across protocol boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking for an address goes through a helper who knows a few other helpers. If one does not know, it points you to a better one, until someone has the answer.

sections.title: The Message Format
sections.content:
Every message has up to five sections: Header, Question, Answer, Authority and Additional. The header is always present and holds an ID that ties replies to queries, a query/response bit, an opcode, flags for authoritative answer (AA), truncation (TC), recursion desired (RD) and recursion available (RA), a response code, and four 16-bit counts. The question has a QNAME, QTYPE and QCLASS. The other three sections are lists of resource records (RRs), each with NAME, TYPE, CLASS, TTL, RDLENGTH and RDATA.

Names are sequences of labels, each a length octet followed by the characters. Labels are limited to 63 octets and a whole name to 255 octets. To save space, a name can end in a two-octet pointer whose top two bits are ones and whose low 14 bits give an offset into the message. Senders may skip compression, but every receiver must understand it.

Messages travel in datagrams, which are limited to 512 octets, with a truncation flag set if a message is longer, or over virtual circuits, which allow up to 65535 octets. On a virtual circuit such as TCP, a 16-bit length is put in front. Datagrams should be kept to simple queries, not maintenance or recursive queries. The Internet uses port 53 for both TCP and UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: Every question and answer uses the same form with the same boxes: a tag to match replies to questions, the question, the answer, and pointers to better helpers.

sections.title: Queries and Resolver Behavior
sections.content:
Three kinds of query are defined. A standard query asks for a resource attached to a domain name. An authoritative server returns the data, a statement that the name does not exist, or a statement that the data does not exist. A server that is not authoritative returns what it has plus records that point to an authoritative server, normally with the addresses of those servers in the additional section. The RFC walks through a mail query for F.ISI.ARPA that first returns a referral and then, from A.ISI.ARPA, an answer.

An inverse query maps a resource to a domain name, for example an address to a name. Results are not guaranteed to be unique or complete, and support is optional, but every server must at least return a Not Implemented error. A completion query expands a partial name such as a shorthand typed by a user, by whole-label matches first and then partial-label matches, for either all candidates or a single best one. Support is optional too.

Recursive service is optional. A client sets RD, and a server that supports recursion sets RA in its responses. Without recursion, the requestor iterates on referrals itself.

A resolver first checks its local database, then looks for the closest known name server, queries one (trying others on failure), caches what it receives, and either returns the answer, returns an error for a nonexistent name, or follows a referral to a closer server.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask 'what is the address of this name?', 'whose address is this?', or 'which name starts like this?'. Helpers either answer, or point you to someone better.

sections.title: Zones and Name Server Maintenance
sections.content:
Zone data originates in text master files, one zone each, which an administrator edits. A zone starts at a node with an SOA record, and its bottom edge is marked by NS records that delegate authority. Other name servers become authoritative for a zone by copying it from the master server over a virtual circuit. The SOA record carries a serial number and the timing parameters: REFRESH, RETRY, EXPIRE and MINIMUM.

When the refresh interval ends, the copy server asks the master for the SOA record. If the SERIAL field matches, the copy is current. If not, it requests the whole zone with an AXFR query, and the master sends it a node at a time, starting and ending with the SOA node. If the serial changed during the transfer, the request is repeated. If the master cannot be reached, the copy keeps retrying at the RETRY interval until EXPIRE passes, after which it must no longer treat its copy as authoritative.

Authoritative and cached data are kept separately, and cached data is never used when authoritative data is available. Updates build a new copy and swap it in under a lock so queries are not disturbed. Cached records expire by TTL; the server does not refresh them.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper keeps a copy of a page from the main book. Every so often it checks the page number and, if the main page changed, copies the new one.

sections.title: Mail Support
sections.content:
The domain system supports mail with two levels of binding. With agent binding, a mailer uses only the part after the at sign as a domain name and sends a MAILA query, which returns MD records (hosts expected to hold the mailbox) and MF records (hosts willing to forward it). These are hints, not definite answers.

With mailbox binding, the whole destination becomes a domain name, with the user part as a single label, and the mailer sends a MAILB query. Possible results are a name error, a Mail Rename (MR) record, a Mailbox (MB) record naming a host, mail group (MG) records for members of a list, or MB together with MG. A MINFO record can name a responsible person and an error mailbox. The memo expects agent binding to come first and mailbox binding to become preferred as organizations convert their mail systems.
sections.plainLanguage: For mail, you can ask which building takes mail for a company, or which exact desk takes mail for one person.

sections.title: Internet Specifics and IN-ADDR
sections.content:
The appendices define syntax and record types. The preferred label syntax is letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter and ending with a letter or digit, up to 63 characters. The A record holds a 32-bit address, and WKS describes well known services by protocol and port bitmap.

For finding the name of an address and the gateways on a network, the special IN-ADDR top-level domain is organized by address with the octets reversed. The address 10.2.0.52 is stored at 52.0.2.10.IN-ADDR, and PTR records point back to host names. Because it is organized by address, the right data can be located without an exhaustive search. The RFC cautions that these records live in different zones from the host's normal name, so they can be inconsistent.
sections.plainLanguage: To find a name from a number, the book has a second index sorted by number, with the number written backwards.

fields.desc: Identifier copied into replies to match them to the query.

fields.desc: 0 for a query, 1 for a response.

fields.name: Opcode
fields.desc: Kind of query, copied into the response.

fields.name: ANCOUNT
fields.desc: Resource records in the answer section.

fields.name: NSCOUNT
fields.desc: Name server records in the authority section.

fields.name: ARCOUNT
fields.desc: Resource records in the additional section.
